newsitem.title: UK: Lira in ERM but lengthy talks worrying - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Lira in ERM but lengthy talks worrying - analysts.

text.p: The lira has made it back into the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) but the protracted nature of this weekend's negotiations has worried European analysts.

The lira rejoined the ERM with a central rate of 990 per mark after two days of talks and amid reports that Italy wanted 1,010 but were prepared to go to 1,000, while other member states, particularly Germany, wanted a much firmer rate of between 950 and 980.
The 990 compromise has left the impression that the road to European monetary union (EMU) in 1999 will perhaps be even more rocky than previously thought, analysts said.
"Pity the weaker nations," said David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Stearns.
"There wasn't this kind of row over the (Finnish) markka joining because at the end of the day it doesn't pose any kind of trade threat to France or Germany."

The Finnish markka joined the ERM in October after a meeting of the EU monetary committee that only lasted a few hours. Saturday's EU committee meeting on the lira ended in deadlock and forced Sunday's meeting of senior ministers in order to resolve the stalemate.

Analysts said problems probably arose because unlike Finland, the Italian economy accounts for a large portion of inter-European trade and for an increasing slice of European markets, so it was obviously a big bone of contention.
They suspected that Sunday's deal was struck on the basis that Italy could not expect much help should the lira get into trouble within the system in the coming months.

"I think this is a case of Italy being allowed to join but being very much isolated in terms of the sort of support it could expect from other countries," said Stephen King, international economist at HSBC Markets.

There is a strong feeling in the market that Germany does not want Italy to be in the first round of EMU and if the lira does get into trouble in the ERM it would perhaps suit the core members' political book not to have to ride to its rescue.
"I have to say I don't think it will last for Italy," King said. "I think they will end up with quite serious problems next year."
To meet the Maastricht critera Italy has to reduce its budget deficit and an easy way to do this would be to slash interest rates.
However, analysts doubt this will be possible with the kind of exchange rate constraint that ERM imposes now in place.

But the simple fact that the negotiations to get the lira back into an exchange rate system with massive 15 percent fluctuation bands took an entire weekend, does not bode well for the countdown to monetary union in 1999, analysts said.
"Rather than big-bang in 1999, it could be big-bustup," Bear Stearns Brown added.
The lira surged to 993 per mark compared with 999.00 before the news and 999.15 in late European trading on Friday.
